We examine whether the conventional differentiation and integration processes preserve the positive definiteness of zonal functions with respect to their angular variable. It turns out that for most scenarios, computing derivatives or integrations of zonal functions results in loss of positive definiteness. Furthermore, even when computing integrations that yield positive definiteness, we observe an increase in the associated parameter d. Nonetheless, specific differentiation cases do maintain positive definiteness and correspond to modifications of the associated differential operator.

Our study delves into theoretical and experimental aspects of space-filling cellular structures known as liquid foams, focusing on how they respond to forces in two and three dimensions. An important parameter in this research is the roughness factor, which measures the ratio of the size of void spaces to solid parts. As the roughness factor increases, foams start to behave more like disordered solids than like bubbly fluids or gas-filled skeletons, leading to novel connections between different scientific fields. This research uses large-scale computer simulations and experimental data from physical foams to examine how these structures move under stress in two dimensions. Through analysis of displacement patterns, we found that there are distinct size groups of motion effects originating from forces applied in different parts of the structure, which can help us understand how information travels within these complex frameworks. A key discovery from this research is that the framework of liquid foams, when viewed through the lens of scaling laws, unifies three previously unrelated behaviors into a coherent framework, which has significant practical applications in designing and utilizing functional foam materials.

Convolutional neural networks are widely used in real-world applications, but they rely heavily on large datasets and powerful computers for training, which can be limiting. These networks are also prone to overconfidence and make incorrect decisions with high certainty when presented with novel or manipulated images. Ensembles are known to improve performance and reliability in computationally intensive tasks, yet their application to CNNs is constrained by the resource-intensive nature of training multiple copies. This research presents a practical guide to developing efficient CNN ensembles that utilize fewer computational resources than traditional ensembles, while also improving the accuracy and reliability of image classification. By leveraging the characteristics of neural networks, a technique called neural ensemble reduction is utilized to create streamlined versions of CNNs in a consistent regulatory framework, allowing for the development of optimized ensembles through the negotiation of targets with an algorithm.

We employ a numerical method based on the finite element approach to examine the effects of membrane tension during a rotating Hele-Shaw process. The analysis considers various rotation rates and distinguishes between low and high tension scenarios. The results show that for both low and high tension cases, four distinct states with corresponding positions of the membrane pose exist, which correspond to configurations observed experimentally. The influence of rotation rate on the stability ranges of these states is determined and expressed in terms of Gouy-Chapman length. The relationship between the states is depicted using a state diagram and includes both reversible and irreversible transitions with corresponding solutions to the Rayleigh criterion. The method used to examine the system's behavior is demonstrated to be fully automated, precise, and capable of handling the large parameter variations required to study the effects of membrane tension during rotation.

A theoretical study of cyclopentadiene (C5H) and cyanocyclopentadiene (CCYC5N) has been undertaken, with comparisons drawn to the well-studied benzene ring. The all-electrons, correlated-electron method has been utilized to examine the electronic structure of these compounds in both their ground and excited states. Four distinct C5H minima have been discovered, with the linear isomer exhibiting the lowest energy, followed by two curved isomers and a cyclopentadienyl radical, the latter of which displays a relatively high barrier to formation. The effects of solvent on the stability of these compounds have been assessed using the conductor-like polarizable solvent model, with predictions made for the infrared spectra of the four minima. Ten valid potential curves have been established for the three lowest-lying electronic states of the cyclopentadienyl radical, enabling the computation of absorption cross-sections and band intensity ratios. The rate of cyclopentadiene production has been estimated at 1.0 x 10-9 s-1 based on the band intensity ratios and infrared spectrum predictions, which when combined with the known rate of CN derivatives results in a cyclopentadiene to cyanocyclopentadiene abundance ratio of approximately 3x10-4. The effects of solvent on these rates have been deemed negligible based on previous research findings. Furthermore, the rate of cyanocyclopentadiene formation is predicted

Standard neural machine translation models train left-to-right but can benefit from look-ahead attention to capture right-to-left dependencies. Such models have shown superior performance in previous works but are computationally expensive due to the need to analyze future inputs during decoding, which slows down translation of new sentences that have not been fully encoded yet. We introduce an efficient right-to-left attention mechanism called Progressive Right-to-Left Attention (PRA) which gradually decouples the decoding from the need to look at future inputs. During the decoding of each word, PRA generates a set of auxiliary queries that replace the need to attend to the remaining unencoded inputs by gradually encoding a subset of them, thus making the set of auxiliary queries grow exponentially as decoding progresses. To control this growth, PRA employs a filter network that selects the most informative inputs to encode, leading to a compact representation of auxiliary queries that enables fast training and decoding. Experimental results on three public sentence-level translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of PRA outperforming the baseline look-ahead attention with minimal computational overhead.

This paper discusses the significance of a language-based approach to evaluating and enhancing technology models, focusing on grid computing as a case study. We argue for adopting a translational method in computer science research and discuss how it can be applied to assess the grid computing research landscape. Our analysis involves examining recent publications to understand current trends and challenges, discussing potential future directions for grid computing, and evaluating the role of formal methods in grid computing research. This paper aims to be a useful resource for those interested in grid computing, whether from a practical or theoretical perspective.

A new proposal for a cosmological model is put forth using the framework of $f(R)$ gravity, which is expressed in the Einstein frame as a model with varying viscosity. This model's development relies on a power-law assumption, which is related to the matter content of the universe, and it is shown that the model's viscosity coefficient is not constant. Solutions are provided for various scenarios, including those related to the behavior of the universe in the matter-dominated era and the big bang singularity. This study also explores the possibility of a non-standard interpretation of the model where the scale factor is not related to physical time, but rather to a higher-dimensional space in a matter-coupled scenario. This leads to solutions where the model is non-singular and consistent with observations, including a consistent expression for the model's viscosity and the occurrence of a type II big bang scenario. This study provides theoretical support for this interpretation and examines the effect of this matter in a higher-dimensional space on the scale factor's evolution in our 3+1 dimensional space. This is also reflected in the behavior of physical quantities and deceleration parameter, which are found to exhibit interesting dynamics in the model.

The $J/$$\psi$ meson's decay into hadrons and semi-leptonic channels is well-established, yet the J/$$\psi$$ to invisible particles' decay remains unmeasured and imposes a stringent limit of 6.6 percent, resulting from hadron and leptonic branches being subtracted from the total J/$$\psi$$ yield in direct dark matter searches. If J/$$\psi$$ invisible decays produce long-lived particles, they could generate significant backgrounds for nucleon scattering off nuclei in direct dark matter experiments, like NA62, NA64, LHCb, FASER, and E141 at the JLab. To assess this risk, we estimate the cross sections for dark matter-nucleon scattering from the J/$$\psi$$ invisible decay are currently constrained and future experiments could lower these limits by up to two orders of magnitude. Nucleon cross sections of $10^{-39}$ to $10^{-40}$ cm$^2$ at a 10 GeV momentum transfer are currently prohibited, with JLab and LHC being the primary sources of searches.

MFSSA is an enhanced version of SSA that leverages multiple datasets to generate robust models, suitable for handling noisy data sets. It employs principal component analysis to create optimized time-domain components that represent meaningful features. Due to its linearity and simplicity, MFSSA is a versatile tool with applications in various fields, including climate pattern extraction from temperature data. In this study, we test the method using synthetic data representing Earth's surface, including remote sensing images and embedded object features. In order to accurately evaluate the algorithm's performance on complex data sets, we develop a new distance metric called MLE distance, which accounts for non-stationarity. Our results demonstrate that MFSSA can accurately reconstruct synthetic images and extract meaningful features, including object positions and sizes. Furthermore, we discover that some components retain frequencies associated with tidal variations.

Let b be a positive integer and consider a random walk in R^b composed of i.i.d. zero-mean increments whose variance is non-degenerate and whose probability density function is smooth. When the random walk is centered at its skew-Hermite class, its long-term behavior can be categorized into three types depending on the value of b: type F for 1 ≤ b ≤ 2, strong law of large numbers when b ≥ 3. A smooth version of this classification is presented for random walks with i.i.d. increments that have k moments, where the asymptotic behavior resembles the standard classification when increments have infinite k moment density.

The efficiency and output quality of plasma sources depend heavily on the balance between their electron temperature and density distributions. To achieve a more accurate understanding of these sources, a novel computational model based on self-consistent fluid equations has been developed. This model provides a faster and more accessible alternative to traditional methods while retaining a high level of accuracy. The validity of this approach has been demonstrated through the replication of results from previous studies, including the replication of a temperature profile previously obtained through molecular dynamics simulations and radio frequency sources. This research paves the way for more complex simulations that can incorporate multielectronic degrees of freedom, enabling the modeling of sources with greater realism.

This paper proposes a novel W-shaped network (WSNet) for efficient automatic nucleus detection, designed to address the limitations of current methods that either require few stages with extensive depth or numerous stages with minimal depth. WSNet introduces a unique framework that combines both aspects into a few shallow stages, effectively enhancing computational performance while maintaining robust feature extraction capabilities. To optimize performance, WSNet incorporates adaptive channels, selectively enhancing relevant features and suppressing redundant information. Furthermore, the network incorporates short-term and long-term memory modules for recursive processing, enabling it to seamlessly integrate local detection with global sequence modeling. Experimentation on three public datasets demonstrates significant F1 score improvements of over 10 points compared to state-of-the-art methods, and a 1.44 nodule per GPU gain of up to 40 nodule/min at high load conditions, showcasing WSNet's superior performance and practical applicability.

For any two representations σ and π in the space of continuous functions from Gl_n(k_s) to the complex numbers, the isomorphism class of σ equals that of π holds if and only if a specific local gamma factor ρ(σ, π) has a rank of zero. This equivalence relationship between rank-zero conditions and isomorphism holds without assuming any additional conjectures or hypotheses. This result holds for representations that appear with finite multiplicity and is valid in both the p-adic and mixed characteristic settings, applicable to odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups.

Recently, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have gained significant attention for their successful application in node classification tasks across various domains, despite their reliance on specific graph-based assumptions. We investigate the mathematical foundations of GCNs, providing a unified framework that demonstrates the relationship between traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as special cases of GCNs. Our analysis specifically examines the GCN normalization method, revealing the equivalence between the standard GCN layer and a combination of a folded Neural Network and a supervised graph convolution operation. Furthermore, under certain conditions, we prove that under the GCN normalization method, a single layer of a GCN is not capable of linearly separating node labels in the feature space. Numerical experiments support these theoretical findings, noting that the performance of GCNs is partly attributed to their ability to transform input data effectively. Our work contributes to the understanding of GCNs, equipping researchers with valuable insights for developing novel and GCN-based networks that leverage both graph structure and node attributes.

A new theory known as "hairy black holes" and derived from the Einstein-Chern-Weil theory will be examined to understand its thermodynamic properties, specifically rotating black holes. Researchers will investigate the transition from general relativity to the theory of Chern-Simons gravity and determine the Chern-Simons three-form's dependence on the horizon's parameters, then calculate the black holes' entropy using the Iyer-Barkov method. The results show that the entropy of these black holes is directly related to the horizon's area, with a coefficient that has a clear geometric meaning. Furthermore, the method used to calculate the entropy can be expressed as an integral over the event horizon, revealing that the Chern-Simons three-form is inherently tied to the horizon's geometry.

Ultrasound elastography is a diagnostic method that visualizes tissue hardness with the aid of ultrasound technology. Precise measurement of local tissue movement through matching of high-frequency data plays a crucial role in reconstructing tissue displacement. Although the accuracy of axial displacement estimation surpasses that of lateral displacement estimation, recent studies have demonstrated improved elastography results with increased focus on lateral estimation. To tackle this challenge, this study explores the effect of estimation precision on reconstruction accuracy via a large-scale analysis of clinical data and presents a new optimal method for balancing axial and lateral displacement estimation. Furthermore, it examines the effect of estimation precision on results with the aid of representative algorithms and large-scale data sets, and presents a precise approach to optimizing axial and lateral estimation performance, and compares it with baseline methods.

Logical pseudocodes fill a middle ground between high-level specifications and formal proofs, focusing on correctness without concern for safety. We explore logical pseudocodes as a tool for writing prominent, easy-to-verifier proofs. A library of logical pseudoproofs for Sequent Calculus was developed using Coq, targeting easy-checking, high-correctness guarantees. The approach is a simple, correct pseudocode translated from Sequent Calculus, with a corresponding library in Coq that validates its correctness at a basic level. This allows correct logical pseudocodes to be treated as correct statements, unlike traditional pseudocodes.

We present a one-pass coreset construction algorithm for the $k$-means clustering problem, utilizing $k^{O(k)}\epsilon^{-2}$ bytes of memory and achieving an approximation within a factor of $(1+\epsilon)$, for small values of $\epsilon$. This achievement is notable, particularly in comparison to prior methods that involved exponential dependencies on $k$ but much greater memory requirements. Our approach improves upon previous one-pass algorithms, such as those by Muthukumar et al. and Woodruff, while maintaining a manageable constant or low polynomial dependence on $k$. Furthermore, our method leverages a novel discretization of Euclidean space, along with a one-pass algorithm to approximate the dimension of the data, enabling the application of coreset techniques. These results primarily hold true in the streaming model, although they also apply to algorithms designed for randomized algorithms.

We applied multi-agent matrix games to enhance Nash Equilibrium Nash Social Welfare Optimization strategies within a fragmented grid world. This method divides the original N-dimensional state space into a manageable two-dimensional subspaces, resolving memory limitations and computational challenges associated with large state spaces. By resolving each subgame independently and aggregating the results, our approach leverages the power of multi-agent matrix games to optimize Nash Equilibrium strategies. This leads to the development of a partition-based multi-agent matrix game framework that guarantees a valid solution to each subgame while maintaining real-time memory efficiency. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in pursuit-evasion situations and provide valuable insights for scalable decision-making in complex multi-agent environments.

The behavior of W and Z bosons in the context of high-energy collisions is being investigated through the application of perturbative QCD to the leading order, followed by a analysis of the first two subleading terms which are universally applicable and not process-specific. This research also involves an examination of a specific process - D0 dijet production at the Tevatron - to provide a practical example of PDF evolution in a spacelike region and utilizes a new set of spacelike NPDFs from the N^2LL resummation of the BDMPS-Z energy loss formalism. This approach accounts for universal corrections and can be used to describe the characteristics of the soft function in a particular type of process - dijet production with a large transverse separation between the two jets. This paper aims to establish a framework for studying color correlations in a real process and provides parton distribution functions (NPDFs) that incorporate the impact of color dynamics on the color dipole evolution. This is a novel contribution to the field and can be used to improve predictions for LHC processes involving energy loss, such as nuclear modification and transverse momentum spectra of hadrons in cold and semicold processes. In multi-task reinforcement learning, a common strategy involves training a single model to generalize across various tasks. However, research indicates that using one unified model can lead to catastrophic interference when tasks require significantly different solutions. We found this result holds true even for simple physical environments using discrete state spaces. To address this issue, we propose training multiple specialized dynamics models that are selected during inference based on the observed transition patterns of new data. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, allowing agents to accurately predict outcomes for both seen and unseen tasks. Furthermore, we found that our method outperforms the traditional approach of a single learned model and allows for faster task adaptation.

Rosser's 1936 incompleteness theorem significantly strengthened Gödel's first incompleteness principle by addressing the issue of self-referential statements and assuming only Consistency as opposed to stronger system requirements.  Even so, the strategy employed by Rosser to achieve this theorem has proven notoriously hard to analyze and apply. Furthermore, the relationship between the statements asserting the incompleteness of formal systems capable of basic arithmetic and the logical level they occupy within $Ardelov$'s tree of theories remains unclear. Our research delves into a step-by-step interpretation of the statement expressing the incompleteness of an effective formal system, for which soundness can be verified according to the conditions set by Dedekind, and which holds true for the vast majority of standard systems of arithmetic. Our primary finding, for which we provide a concise and direct proof, is the following: if an effective formal system is consistent and extends certain minimal arithmetic systems, then Rosser's incompleteness theorem applies; in contrast, if such a system is shown to be inconsistent through proofs of a specific complexity, then the statement expressing the incompleteness of that system may fall outside the $Pi_0^0$-segment of the corresponding logical framework that the system itself requires to be understood.

This research proves a generalized version of Hadamard's three circles theorem specifically for monogenic functions in spaces with more than one dimension. As a result, we derive the consequence that the norm of monogenic functions grows at most exponentially along the z-axis in an cylindrical coordinate system.

Imaging tasks such as tomographic reconstruction can benefit greatly from Bayesian posterior sampling. Currently, GANs have been shown to be effective at generating diverse and realistic samples, and we propose a novel approach called RW-GAN that regularizes conditional Wasserstein distances. This method combines the zero-sum game framework of conditional GANs with a bi-level minimization problem to achieve regularized optimization. theoretically, and numerically we verify that this approach is equivalent to directly solving the conditional Wasserstein GAN, which is non-concave and otherwise difficult to solve. As evidence of its effectiveness, RW-GAN is applied to generate 2D sparse $1/f$ posterior samples in image tomography, and we demonstrate its superiority over conventional regularized approaches by providing a sufficient amount of numerical support.

This research develops a method for identifying linear subspaces within complex fractional order systems that maintain their structure under dynamic changes. The approach involves formulating the requirement for these subspaces to be unalterable under specific conditions, then using a step-by-step process to idenify them. The proposed method is particularly useful for idenifying linear components in fractional order systems and can be applied to create models that preserve key characteristics. The second part of this paper presents examples demonstrating the idenification of these subspaces, including a case where a non-integer order system contains a zero-bias subspace.

Observations of the radio pulsar PSR B1133+16 conducted with the Arecibo Telescope in April 2020 revealed that the plasma within the solar wind is structured like a series of individual screens, each causing the star's radio waves to scatter in a unique way. By pinpointing the location of these screens at distances ranging from 0.7 to 3.4 astronomical units from Earth, researchers were able to determine the position of the plasma itself. In addition to locating the screens, the study also found that they moved at speeds between 37 and 53 kilometers per second during the observations, although these velocities varied over time. The research team was able to map the screens' movements in two dimensions using the difference in arrival times of the scattered signals, but a full understanding of their trajectories in three dimensions would require more observations spread out over longer periods of time. Furthermore, by examining the spread of the signals caused by their motion, researchers were able to gain insights into the size and shape of the screens, which appeared to be between 0.15 and 0.5 astronomical units in size. These findings provide a detailed understanding of how plasma within a few astronomical units of the Sun causes the radio pulses from PSR B1133+16 to behave in a complex way.

This paper proposes a novel cascaded network structure for signal processing, drawing inspiration from the layered composition of certain natural systems. We developed the Cascaded Complex Valued Neural Network (CCVNN) algorithm to optimize signal modeling, with speech as a primary use case due to its cascaded and quasi-periodic characteristics. In a CCVNN framework, multiple convolutional valued neural network (CVNN) modules are arranged in series, and signal periodicity is managed through CVNN components while quasio periodicity is handled through inter-cascaded connections. Evaluating the proposed method on the Libras dataset and the 2020 speech corpus demonstrated CCVNN's superior performance compared to standard CVNN models.

This note delves into the fundamentals of topological Hochschild homology from a specific bicategorical angle, focusing on the application of topological Berstein-Elkalaoui-Mandell theory. It begins by defining the functor F and describing the relevant bicategory, utilizing the concept of a shadow to define topological Hochschild homology. Subsequently, it explains how these definitions reduce to the standard ones. The discussion is enriched with an examination of various properties of topological Hochschild homology, including its behavior under restriction to spherical functors, which leads to the identification of the homology of a point as a specific invariant of a certain bicategory. It also explores the connection between topological Hochschild homology and K-theory, as well as its relation to the Rouse el-Basch homology of a functor. The content is based on the author's research and presentations, particularly at a seminar in topological K-theory in Leipzig.

Pre-trained deep learning models from natural language, speech, and vision domains have shown great success when deployed in resource-sensitive scenarios like zero-shot source localization. Although the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark was introduced recently to standardize evaluation across these benchmarks, the dataset consists of only 155 song sources from the VGG Sound Dataset, limiting its applicability due to the vocal-only nature of these sources. In this release, we have significantly expanded the VGG-SS using the VGG Sound Dataset Test set to include over 9000 labeled sources in the form of short clips, and we have explored several baseline methods for source localization using these new data. By presenting VGG-SS along with expanded datasets, we have made available high-resolution versions of the labels and are encouraging the research community to develop novel methods for source localization that can be evaluated using the new VGG-SS benchmark based on the extended benchmark protocol.

Existing hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (GCNs) based on the Lorentzian metric have primarily focused on enhancing the representation of graph structures, while neglecting the evolution of node features. In this work, we introduce a novel LGCN model that addresses both challenges by unifying them under a single optimization framework. Our model leverages the property that GCNs maximize the Lorentzian inner product between neighboring node features, which serves as a regularizer. Furthermore, our approach is built upon the foundation that hyperbolic graphs GCNs can be viewed as a special instance of LGCNs. We evaluate our model on two synthetic datasets and three hyperbolic graph datasets, and the results show that LGCN outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in link prediction and node classification tasks. Our work provides a new perspective on hyperbolic graph representation learning, demonstrating that it benefits from the unified perspective of the Lorentzian metric.

This research focuses on recovering an source term in an interior region of a domain from the data measured on a boundary in a PDE model describing the flow of a fluid in a channel with time-varying boundary inputs. An key step in proving the interior recovery stability results is an observability inequality which is a variation of a controllability problem for an adjoint PDE. Ultimately, it is shown that the PDE solution corresponds to one with a source term that matches the data from the interior region is uniquely determined and relies on the observability inequality to establish the required estimate.

The article proposes a novel framework for interpreting the Tsallis distribution within sociological systems using a modified approach to expected utility theory. This framework suggests a connection between the characteristic parameter of the Tsallis distribution and Fisk's probability measure in expected utility theory. By redefining probability through a power law transformation, probability judgments and utility preferences can be separated. The model is empirically tested using data on online movie ratings from IMDb, demonstrating that a non-additive expected utility theory can effectively explain the emergence of power law distributions in sociological systems without requiring complex assumptions like multiplicative process models or self-organized criticality. The proposed framework also offers a practical method for estimating the characteristic parameter of the Tsallis distribution from real-world data.

Starting from the action for linearized gravity, a perturbation to the metric is analyzed to determine how it responds to a gravitational wave source in a given background. Initially, this analysis is conducted using the standard $h_{\mu
u}$ degrees of freedom, before a change of variables transforms $h_{\mu
u}$ into a combination of a massless gravitational wave component and a field with two degrees of freedom that resembles a massive spin-2 field. By taking the Fierz-Pauli mass limit, the field theory is solved for its massive spin-2 component, and the resulting equation of motion for $h_{\mu
u}$ is found to be consistent with general relativity, incorporating the mass term and describing the interaction between the massless and massive spin-2 fields. The nonlinear extension of this idea is explored with a perturbative approach in both small mass and small source regimes, and a connection is made with conformal gravity, suggesting a possible link between that theory and the f(R) class of theories.

Quantum statistical mechanics classifies Hamiltonian dynamics into four categories based on the establishment of quantum equilibrium states and their invariance under time evolution. These categories, also applicable to non-Hamiltonian systems, are defined by the simultaneous presence or absence of time-evolution-invariant measures and Hamiltonian dynamics compatible projections of the original system. A research framework is presented that identifies a non-ergodic component in the spectrum of a non-compact invariant subspace of the 3D Boussinesq equations, parameterized by a specific irrational number, within the broader context of non-Hamiltonian dynamics and quantum equilibrium states.

A novel experimental setup using a "bulk" of two-level systems allows for the creation of a system with negative temperature, in which thermal energy behaves like an active component with opposed dynamics to its passive counterpart. With two-level systems being perfectly understood, this framework provides a clear way to visualize and analyze negative temperature. Furthermore, the method used to achieve negative temperature can be applied to a wide range of systems with two-level components. The thermal energy with opposed active and passive characteristics opens up possibilities for applications that could benefit from the properties of negative temperature.

This research extends the scalar singlet model, known as the Geesaw 1 framework, by incorporating a dark sector with complex scalar and fermionic fields. The addition of these fields is intended to enhance the model's capacity to explain dark matter and stabilize its potential, while also conserving a new symmetry, referred to as dark parity, at a high-energy scale. However, this symmetry breaks down at a lower energy level, giving rise to a relationship between dark matter and the scalar component. The research investigates the consistency of this model across various energies, as well as its theoretical stability and capacity to provide explanations for dark matter, the cosmological constant, and the matter-antimatter imbalance. The framework leads to constraints on its parameters through a combination of experimental data, including Higgs boson properties, dark matter abundance, and the matter-antimatter imbalance, as well as predictions for future collisions that may result in the production of scalar and fermionic particles.

We present a comprehensive study of mean-field and beyond mean-field dynamics 
in one-dimensional spinless fermion models containing $p$-orbitals, which contain 
a unique blend of rotation-invariant kinetic energies, effective spin-orbit 
coupling, contact interactions, and crystal field splittings. This approach 
enables an in-depth examination of time-dependent and time-independent properties 
across the full parameter range of these four factors. We analyze both free 
particle dynamics and time-dependent densities for systems with non-interacting 
spin-orbit potentials, and we compare the two approaches for i) the mean-field 
Lowe-and-Kirkland model and for ii) the extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. 
We establish how effective spin-orbit coupling within transition metal oxides 
can both arise and relate to crystal field splitting and occurs irrespective of 
interaction effects. We demonstrate how beyond mean-field dynamics in one 
dimension leads to the effective spin-orbit induced pairing, also known as 
topological superconductivity.

This research focuses on understanding the properties of $I$-functions for toric complete intersections, particularly when they include smooth divisors. We demonstrate that the relative $I$-functions for these toric complete intersections have an organizational structure that can be understood through a smoothing process. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the relative $I$-functions for toric complete intersections with smooth divisors, showing they form a quotient of a more general structure. As a practical application, we utilize these findings to derive the relative Gromov-Witten invariants for specific complex geometric shapes known as hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^{n+1}$ and quadric hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^n$.

A key feature of deep neural networks used in image generation models is their ability to map changes to their corresponding effects, including complex medical conditions. However, because these models often fail to capture the true meaning of their underlying data, it is crucial to explore safe methods of influencing them without releasing harmful representations. In this work, we investigate the effect of latent code changes on how diabetic retinopathy is represented in eye images and, in response, develop a novel approach called Effect-Specific Latent Code Adjustment (ESLA). ESLA, in turn, serves to counteract the effects of latent code manipulation by utilizing a combination of generative adversarial networks and optimization techniques. Evaluations using publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of ESLA in reversing the effects of latent code adjustment and accurately recovering features affected by diabetes-related eye disease.

Our new expert system, ViDaExpert, is designed to guide novice data analysts
through the process of creating effective multidimensional data visualization. This
system takes inspiration from Advanced Decision Support Systems that employ
expert advisors to assist users in complex tasks. To demonstrate the potential
of our approach, we developed a prototype called ViDaExpert, which we evaluated
both objectively and subjectively using two studies. The results highlight both
the value and limitations of using AI to assist with design tasks in scenarios
involving abstract data. Furthermore, our evaluation studies provide insightful
feedback for improving ViDaExpert's capabilities. Open issues and lessons learned
are discussed in the context of future research directions. The code, data sets used,
and presentation files from our studies are available online at this link: https://github.com/visdada/vidaexpert.
